          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. This Court on 21st May 2026 had passed a detailed order. The
said order is reproduced hereinbelow:-
“1.  Rivers  are  the  lifeblood  of
civilization. They provide fresh drinking
water,  sustain  ecosystems  and  drive
economic  growth  through  agriculture,
fisheries,  and  tourism.  It  is  no
coincidence  that  ancient  civilizations
flourished along rivers such as the Nile,
Indus, and Mississippi.
2. Encroachment on the Yamuna riverbed
(particularly  in  fragile  Zone  ‘O’  in
Delhi) along with indiscriminate discharge
of  toxic  effluents  from  illegal
industries,  untreated  sewage  from
unauthorized colonies and mixing of sewage
with rainwater drains has reduced Yamuna
to little more than a sewage channel.
Multiple agencies working in silos have
left  drainage,  sewage,  stormwater,
drinking  water  and  effluent  treatment
systems either non-functional or operating
below capacity. Agencies often work at
cross purposes, even failing to maintain
basic gradients while laying drains within
their  jurisdiction.  Instead  of  curbing
pollution, they are aggravating it. Hard
decisions like removal of encroachments,
closure  of  illegal  industries  and
relocation of unauthorized colonies are
unavoidable.  Such  measures  can  only
succeed if the Union of India, States, and
Union Territories act in concert.
3. At present, however, no State or Union
Territory through which Yamuna flows has a
clear,  coordinated  plan  for  its
conservation,  management,  protection,
revival and pollution control. There is
also no clarity in policy or coordination
3

## Page 19

at the inter-state level.
4. This Court has repeatedly emphasized
the absence of a single, comprehensive
action plan for rejuvenation of Yamuna. A
river is greater than the sum of its
parts. Its revival requires a long-term,
integrated strategy akin to the Namami
Gange Programme. The plan must clearly
state  its  objectives,  implementation
strategy, roles and responsibilities of
each agency, budgetary allocations, and
timelines.  Coordination  and  monitoring
must be entrusted to a single authority.
5. On the previous date of hearing, Mr. K.
Parameshwar, learned Senior Advocate, was
appointed  Amicus  Curiae.  The  Union  of
India has now proposed that the Union Home
Secretary could act as Nodal Officer to
coordinate efforts between States, Union
Territories,  and  the  Centre.  Learned
Amicus Curiae has given a comprehensive
note containing the following suggestions:
“a. The Union of India – coordinated by
Additional Secretary level officers of the
Ministry of Home, Ministry of EF&CC and
Ministry of Jal Shakti, be directed to
urgently call a meeting of the stakeholders
from the States of Uttar Pradesh, Delhi and
Haryana.
b. Direct that in the meeting a proposed
structure/architecture for a nodal planning
and implementing agency (Nodal Agency) be
deliberated and a consensus be arrived at.
It  may  be  kept  in  mind  that  proposed
structure  must  reflect  the  planning,
budgetary,  technical  and  coordination
gaps/challenges involved in the cleaning up
of Yamuna-qua treating effluents discharged
and the treatment of the drains that flow
into Yamuna River.
c.  It  is  expected  that  at  least  some
members/officials must work full time on
coordination  and  implementation  in  the
Nodal Agency.
d. The Nodal Agency is expected to come out
with  full-fledged  action  plan,  across
States for the clean-up of the river Yamuna
with timelines and actionable points.
e. The suggested action points on which
such action plan could be based on are as
follows:
i. Details of cities and towns which are discharging the effluents
in the River Yamuna;
ii. Details of industries which are polluting the Yamuna River in
all of the three states;
iii. GAP Analysis of Industries situated in the entire stretch of
Yamuna River;
iv. Construction of more STPs and availability of the land for the
same;
v. All STPs, drains and CETPS on Yamuna River to be geo-tagged and
4

## Page 20

monitored;
vi. Details of Gram Panchayat and Revenue Villages on the banks of
the Yamuna River;
vii. Wet Lands/Water Bodies along the River Yamuna;
viii. Management of E-Waste, sewage generated from the cities,
Municipal Solid Waste, Bio-medical Waste, Hazardous Waste, E-Waste
and the Industrial waste.
ix. River Water Quality Data to be uploaded on the website.
x. MSW Improvement Action Plan time-line for the Urban Local
Bodies of Department of Urban Development in all of the three
States.
xi. Other relevant information.”
6. Accordingly, this Court constitutes a Committee headed by the Union
Home Secretary, comprising Chief Secretaries of all States and Union
Territories through which Yamuna flows including Secretaries/Heads of
State Pollution Control Boards and the learned Amicus Curiae. The
Committee shall prepare a comprehensive Yamuna Action Plan within eight
(08) weeks. The Home Secretary shall be at liberty to co-opt experts or
other authorities as required.
7. List on 12th August, 2026. The matter to be treated as part heard.”
2. In pursuance to the said order, a Committee was
constituted  under  the  Chairmanship  of  Secretary  of
Ministry of Home Affairs. 
3. This Court on 22nd September 2026 has passed another
order. The said order is reproduced hereinbelow:-
“1. Pursuant to our order dated 12.08.2026, the
Committee has prepared the ‘Yamuna Action Plan’
and  the  same  has  been  submitted  for  our
perusal.
2. In the status note appended to the letter which
forwarded the action plan to the Amicus, it is
mentioned that the ‘Yamuna Action Plan’ does
not have any proposal for removal or relocation
of encroachments/unauthorized structures on the
riverbeds, floodplains or drains falling within
the National Capital Territory of Delhi.
3. At page 112 of the Action Plan, it is mentioned
that  1799  unauthorized  colonies  have  been
identified for which integrated sewerage system
is being developed and the work to the extent
of 73% is complete. Rest is at various stages
of implementation.
4. We notice that in the Master Plan for Delhi-
2047, a special initiative for rejuvenation of
river Yamuna and its floodplains is envisaged.
However,  what  is  striking  is  that  it
dichotomizes floodplains by earmarking active
floodplains. On what basis floodplains have
been differentiated by treating some as active
needs to be explained.
5. Further,  how  many  unauthorized  colonies
5

## Page 21

identified are located over the floodplains
must be disclosed so that we can assess whether
the action plan is one which would be effective
in serving the avowed purpose.
6. Additionally, to have a clear understanding of
the  action  plan  and  the  requisite  steps
proposed  thereunder,  we  would  require  a
representative  from  the  Ministry  of  Home
Affairs to make a Power Point Presentation on
the action plan and the various steps envisaged
thereunder. Learned Amicus has suggested that
it can be arranged on 07.10.2026 at 4.00 pm. We
accept  the  suggestion.  Let  necessary
arrangements be made for the same on 07.10.2026
at 4.00 pm. 
7. Besides, we would like clarity on the issue as
to whether the Master Plan for Delhi-2047 is in
sync with the ‘Yamuna Action Plan’ which has
been placed before us.”
4. On 7th October 2026, this Court received a detailed
presentation  of  the  ‘Yamuna  Action  Plan’.  The
‘Recommendations at a Glance’ in the said Plan read as
under:-
“Recommendations at a Glance
15.1 Domestic Sewage Treatment
 A total of 20 existing STPs will be upgraded to comply
with the notified discharge standards. Their cumulative
treatment capacity will increase from 867.1 MLD to
1,192.16 MLD. State-wise enhanced capacities are as
follows:
o Delhi: from 358.66 MLD to 640.14 MLD
o Haryana: from 284 MLD to 304 MLD
o Uttar Pradesh: from 223 MLD to 245 MLD
o Himachal Pradesh: from 1.44 MLD to 3.02 MLD
 A total of 125 new STPs, with a cumulative treatment
capacity of 4,401.30 MLD, will be established across
the Yamuna basin:
o Delhi: 42 STPs (2,258.65 MLD)
o Uttar Pradesh: 47 STPs (1,490.70 MLD)
o Haryana: 18 STPs (621 MLD)
o Uttarakhand: 18 STPs (30.95 MLD)
15.2 Drain Interception and Treatment
 A  total  of  520  drains,  currently  discharging
approximately  9,666.81  MLD  of  wastewater  into  the
Yamuna  and  its  tributaries,  will  be  intercepted,
diverted and connected to treatment infrastructure to
prevent the discharge of untreated wastewater into the
river.
6

## Page 22

15.3 Industrial Effluents
 Twelve  existing  CETPs  located  in  Delhi  and  Uttar
Pradesh will be upgraded to comply with prescribed
standards.  Following  upgradation,  their  cumulative
treatment capacity will be 82.4 MLD. The reduction from
the existing capacity of 160.8 MLD due to low flow in
CETPs.
 Twelve new CETPs, with a cumulative treatment capacity
of 187.25 MLD, will be established in Haryana to
strengthen industrial wastewater management. 
15.4 Municipal Solid Waste
 A comprehensive programme for municipal solid waste
management  will  be  implemented  across  the  basin,
including:
o Establishment of 10 new MSW processing plants with a
cumulative  processing  capacity  exceeding  565  TPD
(Capacity of 565 TPD is proposed for 6 SWM plants
only);
o Establishment of two Material Recovery Facilities
(MRFs) at Raya and Dankaur with a combined capacity
of 10 TPD;
o Construction  of  seven  compost  pits  at  Tundla,
Auraiya,  Jalaun,  Deoband,  Khair,  Mau  (Chitrakoot
Dham) and Rajpur with a combined capacity of 63 TPD;
o Development  of  two  legacy  waste  remediation
facilities at Barkot and Vikasnagar; and
o Establishment of integrated solid waste management
systems across 33 urban local bodies in Haryana.
 Additional measures include:
o Removal of floating waste from drains;
o Installation of waste collection bins at vulnerable
locations;
o Enforcement  actions,  including  imposition  of
penalties for violations; and
o Information,  education  and  communication  (IEC)
campaigns  to  promote  responsible  waste  disposal
practices.
15.5 Dairy Waste
 A total of 23 biogas plants will be established to
process cattle waste:
o Uttar Pradesh: 12 plants
o Delhi: 8 plants
o Haryana: 3 plants
 These facilities will have a cumulative processing
capacity of 4,208.5 TPD.
15.6 Biomedical Waste
 Biomedical  waste  management  will  be  strengthened
through  expansion  of  treatment  facility  coverage,
7

## Page 23

regular inspections, improved tracking mechanisms and
continued  monitoring  to  ensure  safe  collection,
transportation, treatment and disposal.
15.7 E-Waste
 An E-Waste Eco Park with a processing capacity of
51,000 TPA will be established at Holambi Kalan, Delhi,
to strengthen scientific recycling and disposal of
electronic waste.
15.8 Hazardous Waste
 Hazardous waste management will be strengthened through
enhanced  awareness  programmes  and  comprehensive
tracking through the National Hazardous Waste Tracking
System (NHWTS).
15.9 Restoration of Water Bodies
 A total of 270 water bodies, comprising 13 ponds and
257 wetlands and floodplain water bodies, will be
conserved,  rejuvenated  and  restored  to  enhance
ecological resilience, groundwater recharge and basin
health.
15.10 Increasing Environmental Flows (E-Flows) in the
Yamuna
Key interventions proposed for augmenting environmental
flows include:
 Time-bound completion and commissioning of the Lakhwar,
Renukaji and Kishau dam projects;
 Completion of repair and lining works on the Delhi Sub-
Branch Canal; and
 Discharge of treated water from the Yamuna Vihar and
Coronation Pillar STPs into the Yamuna at Wazirabad.
 Notify Yamuna e-flows by Dec 2026 and designate CWC for
monitoring and compliance.
15.11 Safe Reuse of Treated Water (SRTW)
Key recommendations include
 Aligning all Yamuna Basin states with the National
Framework for Safe Reuse of Treated Water (NF-SRTW) and
notifying updated reuse policies by December 2026 to
institutionalize treated wastewater reuse.
 Mandating the use of treated wastewater by eligible
thermal power plants and promoting its use in industry,
agriculture, construction, and urban applications to
reduce freshwater dependence.
 Achieving  NF-SRTW  reuse  targets  by  ensuring  safe
collection, treatment, and reuse of at least 30% of
used water by 2030 and 50% by 2035. 
15.12 Online Monitoring of STPs and data Dissemination on
Ganga Pulse Public Portal
8

## Page 24

Key recommendations include
 Equip all STPs above 1 MLD in Yamuna districts with
Online Continuous Effluent Monitoring Systems (OCEMS)
by December 2026.
 Integrate OCEMS data from all eligible Yamuna STPs with
the Ganga Pulse Portal and respective State Portals by
March 2027
 Strengthen  continuous  monitoring  of  key  effluent
quality parameters to improve STP efficiency, ensure
regulatory compliance, and support river water quality
restoration.
15.13  Governance,  Monitoring  and  Institutional
Coordination
Implementation  of  the  Action  Plan  will  be  monitored
through four institutional mechanisms:
1. The Union Home Minister;
2. The Union Home Secretary;
3.  The  High-Level  Committee  chaired  by  the  Chief
Minister of Delhi; and
4.  The  Executive  Committee  chaired  by  the  Chief
Secretary of Delhi, along with similar monitoring
mechanisms established by the other basin states.
These  institutional  arrangements  will  ensure  regular
review, inter-governmental coordination, timely resolution
of implementation bottlenecks and effective monitoring of
progress.”
5. This Court finds that the Yamuna Action Plan is a
significant  step  forward,  inasmuch  as  it  identifies
domestic sewage as the single largest source of pollution
entering the river Yamuna. The Plan provides for the
construction of 125 (One Hundred Twenty-Five) new Sewage
Treatment  Plants,  12  (Twelve)  new  Common  Effluent
Treatment Plants, 10 (Ten) new Municipal Solid Waste
Plants and 23 (Twenty-Three) Bio-Gas Plants, besides the
upgradation of existing plants of the same kind.
6. During the presentation, the Court pointed out a few
9

## Page 25

contradictions in the draft Yamuna Action Plan submitted
to this Court. For instance, the Plan does not propose
the removal of encroachments on water bodies and wetlands
alongside Zone ‘O’, on the ground that they are free of
encroachments. However, Annexure-9 to the Draft Yamuna
Action Plan, prepared by the NCT of Delhi, marks all
thirty-five water bodies and wetlands in Zone ‘O’ as
“Yes” for encroachment. Further, although the Plan states
that twenty-eight of the thirty-seven existing Sewage
Treatment Plants in Delhi meet the standards stipulated
by the Central Pollution Control Board in its report at
Annexure V, states that none of these Plants meets all
the prescribed standards and that only five meet the
bacteriological limit.
7. This Court is of the opinion that ‘everything that is
wrong with civic administration in the towns, cities and
villages  situated  along  the  banks  of  the  river  is
reflected in the poor health of the river and in the 520
(five hundred twenty) drains’ that discharge wastewater
into the Yamuna. This is why, despite huge sums being
spent on cleaning the river, pollution in the Yamuna has
only increased.
10

## Page 26

8. This Court is of the view that industrial pollution
and untreated sewage must be curtailed, if not stopped
altogether, at the source. Where that is not possible,
the  sewage  must  first  be  tapped  and  then  treated.
However, tapping will remain a challenge in absence of a
robust sewage system and due to joining of storm-water
and sewage drains. This Court is further of the opinion
that it would be difficult, if not impossible, for civic
authorities  to  tap  sewage  in  most  illegal  and
unauthorised colonies built on encroached land, since
they have not been built on a grid layout and have hardly
any space for laying a sewage system.
9. This Court is also of the view that unless illegal
and unauthorised colonies, JJ clusters on the drains as
well as on the river bed are removed after rehabilitating
their occupants, their sewage will continue to pollute
the river at the source.
10. There  are  also  a  large  number  of  illegal  and
unaccounted-for  dairies  for  instance  in  Delhi,  which
would not benefit from the setting up of the proposed
Bio-Gas Plants in authorised dairies alone.
11

## Page 27

11. This Court is of the opinion that Zone ‘O’, as
defined in the Delhi Master Plan 2047, should not only be
maintained and protected as a ‘Green’ Zone but should
also be extended upstream and downstream if feasible,
that is, from the source of the river Yamuna to its
confluence with the river Ganga. No permanent structure,
except green parks and essential public infrastructure
projects, should be allowed to be constructed in future
in the said or extended Zone. Even for recreational and
tourism purposes, only semi-permanent structures, such as
cycling  and  walking  tracks,  should  be  permitted;
permanent structures may be constructed only outside Zone
‘O’ and that too at a suitable height. Efforts should be
made to remove all structures existing in Zone ‘O’, or in
the proposed extended Zone, in accordance with the extant
law and after allocating alternative accommodation to the
occupants, where they are so entitled. After all, the
river Yamuna must have space to meander and change its
course, if it so chooses. 
  
12. As pointed out in the order dated 21st May 2026, a
‘river is greater than the sum of its parts’.  At this
juncture it is important to note that when several States
12

## Page 28

share one river, it is not enough for each State to only
look after its own stretch, the river has to be treated
as a single, shared resource that all of them are jointly
responsible for. At the same time, it would be unfair to
hold every State to an identical standard, regardless of
how much pollution they actually contribute or how much
capacity they have to deal with it. This balance, which
is a joint responsibility for the river as a whole,
combined with individual obligations calibrated to each
State’s own contribution and capacity, is what has come
to be known internationally as the doctrine of Common but
Differentiated Responsibilities (“CBDR”). This principle
was articulated in Principle 7 of the Rio Declaration on
Environment and Development, 1992, and has since been
carried  forward,  with  the  added  idea  of  “respective
capabilities,” into the UNFCCC (1992), the Kyoto Protocol
(1997) and the Paris Agreement (2015). In essence, it has
two  parts  that  must  work  together:  a  common  part
(everyone owes a duty to the shared resource) and a
differentiated part (how much each one owes depends on
their share of the problem and their ability to fix it).
13. It is important to note that the  ‘common’ part of
13

## Page 29

this  principle  is  just  as  important  as  the
“differentiated” part, and that this is how CBDR ought to
be applied to the Yamuna. The principle should not be
understood as permission to simply divide the river into
separate State-wise segments, with each State answerable
only for the water within its own borders and indifferent
to what happens once it crosses into the next State. The
Yamuna, as stated above, is one continuous ecosystem
running through several States/UTs, and the “common” part
of CBDR requires that it continue to be protected as one
single resource instead of a set of disconnected State-
wise problems. It is only once this shared responsibility
is accepted that the “differentiated” part follows and
accordingly, each State’s specific obligation can then be
calibrated to how much pollution it contributes and what
capacity  it  has  to  deal  with  it.  For  instance,  by
requiring that the quality of the river water leaving a
State cannot be worse than the quality at which it
entered. However, no State’s responsibility should be
treated as limited to, or satisfied merely by, what
happens  within  its  own  stretch  of  the  river.  This
responsibility  operates  in  three  stages:  first,
preventing  pollution  before  it  occurs;  second,  if
14

## Page 30

pollution does occur, bearing the cost of cleaning it up;
and third, restoring the river ecologically where damage
has already been done.
14. This ‘common system’ reading finds direct guidance
from  the  River  Ganga  (Rejuvenation,  Protection  and
Management)  Authorities  Order,  2016,  which,  under
paragraph  4(i),  lays  down  as  the  foremost  governing
principle that ‘the River Ganga shall be managed as a
single  system.’ Since  Yamuna  is  one  of  the  Ganga’s
principal tributaries, this principle extends with equal
force to it as the 2016 Order itself contemplates that a
river  and  its  tributaries  must  be  governed  as  one
integrated  system.  Therefore,  any  order  apportioning
liability on the States for pollution of the Yamuna ought
to expressly adopt this principle-based, common-system
approach,  rather  than  a  disaggregated,  State-by-State
model of responsibility.
15. Consequently,  a  multi-faceted  approach  must  be
adopted  if  the  authorities  wish  to  clean  the  river
Yamuna, rather than an action plan that concentrates only
on  the  construction  of  additional  Sewage  Treatment
Plants, Decentralised Sewage Treatment Plants and Bio-Gas
15

## Page 31

Plants.
16. This Court is, however, cognizant of its limitations,
as it is neither a city planner nor an expert body. It is
for the civic administrators to prepare a plan to clean
the river Yamuna. This Court considers it appropriate to
give the administrators the power and flexibility to do
their jobs, while holding them accountable if they fail
to achieve results. To that end, this Court proposes to
lay  down  a  broad  test  and  to  levy  fines  on  those
States/Union Territories that fail in their duty to check
pollution  of  the  river  Yamuna,  whether  through
inefficiency or for lack of the political will to take
hard decisions.  This Court is of the view that this
approach will put an end to the defence of ‘passing the
buck’.
17. For this purpose, the Central Pollution Control Board
is directed to place before this Court the composition
and  properties  of  the  water,  including  its  chemical
composition and parameters such as Biochemical Oxygen
Demand  (BOD),  Chemical  Oxygen  Demand  (COD),  Fecal
Coliform and Total Suspended Solids (TSS) at the points
where  the  river  Yamuna  and  the  major  drains  (that
16

## Page 32

ultimately flow into it) enter and exit each State/Union
Territory as well as District within the State/Union
Territory.
18. This  Court  is  informed  that  presently,  Central
Pollution Control Board is monitoring River Yamuna at the
points  where  it  enters  and  exits  each  State/Union
Territory, including the major tributaries flowing into
the river, as well as at the entry and exit points of
districts within the respective States/Union Territories
on a quarterly basis. Further monitoring of major inter-
state drains may also be undertaken at an identified
frequency.  Parallel samples collected at the same time
may be analysed simultaneously by established institutes
like  IIT  to  ensure  independent  verification  of  the
results.
19. If the water quality deteriorates on any parameter
while flowing through, or exiting a State/Union Territory
or a District therein, then that State/Union Territory or
District within the State/Union Territory shall be held
accountable and penalised. The said compensation/ fine
shall be deposited with the Registry of this Court. The
Central Pollution Control Board to suggest formula for
computation  of  fine/compensation.  The  States/Union
17

## Page 33

Territories shall be at liberty to recover such fines,
after holding an inquiry, from the polluter as well as
officials who were remiss in performing their duties.
 
20. The  Central  Pollution  Control  Board  shall  also
investigate, inquire and submit a detailed report to this
Court with respect to any incident of pollution in the
river Yamuna like dying of fish or floating of white foam
on surface or  eutrophication or algal bloom or increase
in BOD, COD, TSS levels. The report should specifically
mention  the  cause  of  such  an  incident  or  spike  in
pollution  levels  as  well  remedial  measures  to  be
undertaken.
21. To ensure that in the meantime existing STPs and
CETPs operate at full capacity, it is directed that every
STP, CETP and Government-commissioned biogas plant shall
install  tamper-proof  smart  energy  meters  within  one
month. Every STP and CETP shall install an inflow meter
at the inlet and an outflow meter with continuous sensors
at the point of final discharge, whether into the river
or into a drain. The sensors shall record the volume
discharge  and  the  levels  of  pH,  BOD,  COD,  TSS  and
ammoniacal nitrogen, while fecal coliform shall be tested
weekly in an accredited laboratory.
18

## Page 34

22. All readings shall be uploaded live, plant-wise on
the websites of the Central Pollution Control Board and
the  State  Pollution  Control  Board/Pollution  Control
Committee, so that each plant’s hours of operation, power
drawn,  volume  treated  and  quality  of  discharge  and
thereby  each  operator’s  performance  can  be  tracked.
Biogas plants shall in addition record the waste received
and the gas produced. The meters shall be calibrated
annually by an accredited laboratory and any break in the
data  feed  exceeding  24  (twenty-four)  hours  shall  be
presumed to be non-operation of the plant unless the
operator proves otherwise.
23. This  Court  is  informed  that  presently,  Delhi
Pollution  Control  Committee  is  in  the  process  of
installing Real-time Water Quality Monitoring Stations
(‘RTWQMS’) at identified locations along the River Yamuna
and major drains within the Delhi stretch. Similarly,
other State Pollution Control Boards/Pollution Control
Committees must also undertake installation of RTWQMS at
identified locations along the river and major drains
within  their  respective  jurisdictions.  It  is  further
directed that the real-time water quality data generated

through  these  stations  shall  be  shared  with  Central

24. It is further directed that the Central Pollution

b) recover environmental compensation from the operator

Further, a dedicated portal shall be developed to monitor

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
I.A. Nos. 40499, 30884, & 40488 of 2025 along with CEC Report No.
33 of 2026
1. These  applications  have  been  filed  by  Administrative
Commandant, Station Headquarters, Mathura Cantt. on behalf of
Headquarters, 99 Artillery Brigade and its allied units, seeking
permission for felling of 60 trees falling within the proposed
construction area of Phase-I of the Key Location Plan at Mathura
Military Station.
3

## Page 56

2. This Court, vide order dated 22.04.2025, referred the matter
to the CEC with a direction to the Applicant to disclose the trees
required  to  be  felled  for  all  three  phases.  The  Applicant,
thereafter, filed IA No. 30884 of 2025 stating that plans for
Phase-II and III are yet to crystallize and sought independent
consideration of Phase-I.
3. Consequently, the CEC had submitted Report No.6 of 2026 dated
20.02.2026 recommending felling of 44 trees (instead of 60 trees),
subject to the following conditions as recorded in paragraph 17 of
the report.
“17…………….xxx………...xxx…………….xxx
a) The Applicant shall undertake compensatory plantation
of  not  less  than  550  saplings,  in  terms  of  the
undertaking submitted, and shall ensure their maintenance
and survival for a minimum period of five (05) years. The
plantation shall be carried out within the Applicant’s
Campus, the KML file of which shall be shared with the
CEC. 
b) The felling of trees shall be permitted only after the
aforesaid compensatory plantation has been carried out
and duly verified by the Forest Department. 
c) In addition to the aforesaid compensatory plantation,
the Applicant shall undertake plantation of at least
1,000  saplings  of  the  following  native  species  at
appropriate locations within its campus, in consultation
with the Divisional Forest Officer, Mathura, and shall
maintain the same for a period of five (05) years:
•  100  trees  each  of  Ficus  religiosa,  Ficus
benghalensis, and Ficus virens. (Total 300 Ficus
species); 
4

## Page 57

• 500 trees of Azadirachta indica (Neem), Terminalia
arjuna  (Arjun),  Butea  monosperma  (DhaklPalash),
Zizyphus  mauritiana  (Ber),  and  Mangifera  md/ca
(Mango);
• 200 trees of Bauhinia variegata (kachnar) and
Cassia  fistula  (Amaltas),  which  are  pollinator-
friendly and flowering native species. 
d)  The  Chairman,  TTZ  Authority  shall  ensure  strict
compliance  with  all  the  conditions  imposed  by  this
Hon’ble Court and further ensure that no trees other than
those expressly permitted by this Hon’ble Court are
felled.  In  the  event  of  felling  or  damage  to  any
additional tree, a penalty of Rs. 1,00,000/- (Rs. One
Lakh  only)  per  tree  shall  be  recoverable  from  the
Applicant.”
4. IA No. 30884 of 2025 was disposed of on 03.09.2026 after
recording a statement on behalf of the applicant that the aforesaid
conditions imposed by CEC have been complied with. The CEC,
however, was subsequently directed to independently verify the said
compliance.
5. Thereupon, CEC has submitted Report No.33 of 2026 dated
30.10.2026, inter alia, pointing out that the Divisional Director,
Social Forestry Division, Mathura inspected the site on 27.08.2026,
and CEC independently inspected it on 23.09.2026, finding that all
1,550 saplings (550 compensatory and 1,000 additional saplings of
the  prescribed  species)  were  present,  alive,  healthy,  and
adequately protected. Condition No.17(d) stipulated in the Report
No. 6 of 2026 dated 20.02.2026 is yet to operate, as no felling has
5

## Page 58

taken  place.  The  CEC  has  accordingly  made  the  following
recommendations:
“5. In view of the above, the CEC submits that the
Applicant has complied with the conditions stipulated in
paragraphs 17(a), 17(b) and 17(c) of CEC Report No. 06 of

additional plantation, as independently verified by the
CEC  during  its  site  inspection  on  23.09.2026.
Accordingly, the CEC respectfully recommends that this
Hon’ble Court may consider granting permission to the
Administrative Commandant, Station Headquarters, Mathura
Cantt.,  for  felling  of  44  (forty-four)  trees,  as
identified by the CEC in its Report No. 06 of 2026,
falling within the proposed construction area of Phase-I
of the Key Location Plan (KLP) accommodation at Mathura
Military Station, subject to strict compliance with the
conditions stipulated in the aforesaid CEC Report, the
directions of this Hon’ble Court and all applicable
statutory requirements.”
6. Ms. Liz Mathew, learned Senior Counsel and Amicus Curiae, has
also submitted a self-explanatory note where she has recommended
that permission may be accorded to the applicant to fell the 44
trees, subject to strict compliance with the continuing obligation
to maintain the saplings for five years and the penalty under
Condition 17(d) of Report No. 6 of 2026. The said condition, as
reproduced above, specifies that no additional tree shall be
felled, and in the event any such felling or damage takes place,
there shall be a penalty of Rs.1 lakh per tree on the applicant.
7. Subject to the conditions reproduced above, which are to be
followed and complied with, the application(s) are allowed, and

## Page 59

necessary permission for felling of 44 trees is accorded. The

8. These applications have been filed by Rajasthan State Road
Development and Construction Corporation Limited, seeking felling
of 401 trees for widening and strengthening of BOT Road, Bharatpur-
Bayana-Gangapur-Bhadoti  Road  from  KM  7/0  (Sewar)  to  33/055
(Salabad). The matter was referred to the CEC for examination vide
order dated 24.01.2025. The CEC thereafter submitted Report No.64
of 2025 dated 27.11.2025, recommending felling of 236 trees (215
green and 21 dry), against the original request of 418 trees. This
permission had been accorded subject to the conditions as contained
in paragraph 15 of the said report. The 215 green trees comprise
trees on the proposed road (33), within 0-50 cm of its edge (66),
and leaning towards the road (116). The CEC had also recorded that
14 of the originally enumerated green trees, and 4 of the 17 dry
trees, were missing.
9. Thereafter, vide order dated 03.09.2026, this Court noted the
Applicant-Corporation’s submission that at least 335 trees were
required to be felled for widening the road from 7 to 10 meters.
The  Applicant  was  directed  to  comply  with  the  compensatory
afforestation condition and file a compliance affidavit. The CEC
was accordingly directed to reconsider the request for felling of
335 trees. 
7

## Page 60

10. In deference thereto, CEC has filed Report No.34 of 2026 dated
02.11.2026, observing that the widening of 10 meters was part of
the original proposal and had already been accounted for. The
additional requirement arises because the Applicant has since
modified the road design, increasing the paved shoulders from 50 cm
to 100 cm on either side of the road for safety, and has also
sought felling of 99 additional trees on that account. Upon
inspection, the CEC found that 6 of these trees can be saved, and
recommended felling of 329 trees, with the following conditions
contained in paragraph 9 of the Report.
“9………….the CEC recommends that this Hon’ble Court may
consider granting permission for felling of 329 trees
(308 green and 21 dry), comprising the 236 trees (215
green and 21 dry) recommended earlier and 93 out of 7 99
additional green trees sought by the Applicant, for the
work of widening and strengthening of the Bharatpur-
Bayana-Gangapur Bhadoti Road from KM 7/0 (Sewar) to KM
33/055 (Salabad), falling within the Tai Trapezium Zone
(TTZ). The Applicant had thus sought permission for a
total of 335 trees: however, the CEC has recommended
felling of only 329 trees, as 6 of the additional green
trees can be saved. The permission for felling of 329
trees may be granted subject to the following conditions:
i) Compensatory plantation of 4,180 trees of indigenous
species,  as  committed  by  the  Applicant,  shall  be
undertaken by the Divisional Forest Officer, Bharatpur,
at the cost of the Applicant on the land identified for
this purpose in Village Katariyapur, District Bharatpur.
ii)  The  total  area  of  4.5  hectares  identified  for
compensatory plantation in District Bharatpur shall be
notified as Protected Forest by the State Government
8

## Page 61

within six months, and compliance in this regard shall be
filed before the CEC.
iii) The boundary of the compensatory plantation site
shall be secured with a six-feet-high chain-link fence
fixed on a two-feet-high concrete wall so as to protect
the young saplings from grazing by cattle and other
animals.
iv) Provision for proper watering of the planted saplings
during summer and their maintenance for a period of ten
years shall be included in the plantation estimate to
ensure a better survival rate.
v)  The  funds  required  for  raising  the  compensatory
plantation,  including  the  cost  of  fencing  and
maintenance, as estimated by the State Forest Department,
shall be deposited by the Applicant with the Divisional
Forest Officer, Bharatpur, in an interestbearing bank
account before any permission is granted for felling of
the trees by the Forest Department.
vi) In addition to the aforesaid compensatory plantation,
upon completion of the road-widening work, both sides of
the road shall be planted by the Forest Department with
tall saplings of suitable indigenous species, such as
Ficus religiosa (Pipal), Holoptelea integrifolia (Papdi),
Ficus virens (Pakar), Ficus racemosa (Gular), Azadirachta
indica  (Neem),  Butea  monosperma  (Dhak),  Phyllanthus
emblica  (Aonla),  Terminalia  bellirica  (Baheda),
Terminalia chebula (Harad), Bauhinia variegata (Kachnar),
Syzygium  cumini  (Jamun),  Terminalia  arjuna  (Arjun),
Albizia lebbeck (Sins) and Dalbergia sissoo (Sheesham),
at a spacing of 5 meters. The saplings shall be at least
8-10 feet in height and shall be protected by brick or
iron tree guards. The entire cost of plantation and
subsequent  maintenance  shall  be  deposited  by  the
9

## Page 62

Applicant  with  the  Forest  Department  before  any
permission is granted for felling of trees.
vii) The Forest Department shall undertake an extensive
exercise to identify the missing trees and submit its
findings to the CEC.
viii) The Chairman, TTZ Authority, while ensuring strict
compliance  with  all  the  conditions  imposed  by  this
Hon’ble Court, shall also ensure that no trees other than
those permitted to be felled by this Hon’ble Court is
felled or damaged during the execution of the project. In
case  any  additional  tree  is  accidentally  felled  or
damaged, a penalty of Rs. 1,00,000/- (Rupees One Lakh
only) per tree shall be recovered from the Applicant.
ix) The Applicant shall also comply with the directions
contained in paragraph 31 of the order dated 03.09.2026
passed by this Hon’ble Court and file the requisite
compliance affidavit.”

 (arising out of SLP (Crl.) No. 18320/2026)
MOHAMMAD KAIF APPELLANT(S)
               VERSUS
STATE OF CHHATTISGARH RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The  appellant,  Mohammad  Kaif,  is
aggrieved by the denial of regular
bail by the High Court of Chhattisgarh
at  Bilaspur,  vide order  dated
14.05.2026  passed  in  MCRC  No.
3387/2026. He seeks bail in relation
to First Information Report (FIR) No.
391/2025,  registered  with  Police
Station–Chhawani, Durg, Chhattisgarh,
for  the  offences  punishable  under
Sections 20(b), 2(c) and 27(a) of the
Narcotic  Drugs  and  Psychotropic
   1

## Page 97

Substances Act, 1985. 
3. The appellant, Mohammad Kaif, has been
in custody since 24.07.2025. 
4. Counter affidavit filed by the State
of Chhattisgarh states to the effect
that the appellant and the co-accused
were standing on the National Highway
together  and  the  quantity  of
contraband substance, namely,  Ganja,
seized from them would be more than
the commercial quantity of 20 Kgs,
when  put  together.  However,  the
counter affidavit does not indicate as
to on what basis the appellant has
been clubbed with the co-accused and
as to whether there was any meeting of
minds  between  them.  It  is  for  the
State to establish this fact during
trial. We are further informed that
chargesheet has already been filed but
the trial has not begun. There is,
therefore, no possibility of the trial
concluding any time soon in the near
future.
   2

## Page 98

5. In these circumstances, we are of the
opinion that no grounds are made out
for  continued  incarceration  of  the
appellant,  Mohammad  Kaif,  at  this
stage,  pending  completion  of  the
trial.
6. Accordingly,  we  accept  the  present
appeal and direct that the appellant,
Mohammad Kaif, shall be released on
bail  in  connection  with  the
aforestated FIR on such appropriate
terms and conditions as may be fixed
by the Special Court.
7. In addition, the appellant, Mohammad
Kaif,  shall  cooperate  during  the
course of the trial and shall not take
undue adjournments. 
8. The impugned order is set aside and
the  appeal  is  allowed  in  the
aforestated terms. 
9. We clarify that we have not made any
observations/comments on the merits of
the case and any observation made in
   3

## Page 99

this  order  is  meant  only  for  the
limited purpose of grant of bail.
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall
stand disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Heard Mr. Yatin Oza, learned Senior Counsel appearing for the
applicant in Miscellaneous Application No. 3299 of 2026; Mr. Shyam
Divan, learned Senior Counsel appearing for the respondent-HDFC
Bank  Limited,  the  original  respondent  in  the  Special  Leave
Petition; and Mr. Nachiketa Joshi, learned Senior Counsel appearing
for the Bankruptcy Trustee, who was the petitioner in the original
Special Leave Petition.
2. The present Miscellaneous Application has been filed seeking
clarification of the order dated 01.10.2026 to the effect that the
said order does not preclude the applicant from placing his case
before the learned Mediator.
3. Further, it is prayed that a clarification be issued to the
effect that the order dated 01.10.2026 does not preclude the
continuation of Commercial Suit No. 157 of 2016.
4. The Special Leave Petition itself arose under the following
circumstances:-
In a pending suit filed by the applicant/Respondent no.2, Mr.
Bhupendra Jivrajbhai Surani, against the HDFC Bank, the Bankruptcy
Trustee, Mr. Alan Chung Wah Tang, sought to be impleaded as a
plaintiff on the ground that the plaintiff had been declared
bankrupt and the assets, including the shares in question, had
vested in the Bankruptcy Trustee.
We are not concerned with the other details of the suit for

## Page 122

3
the purpose of the present proceedings.
The HDFC Bank, which is the defendant in the suit, filed
Notice of Motion No. 763 of 2019 along with Interim Application No.
4412 of 2026, seeking to restrain the Bankruptcy Trustee from
proceeding with the proceedings in Action No. 473 of 2026 pending
before the High Court of the Hong Kong, Special Administrative
Region(SAR).
On 24.08.2026, the learned Single Judge of the High Court
directed  that  the  Bankruptcy  Trustee  and  the  authorized
representative Mr. Vinod Kaushik, be restrained from proceeding
with the Hong Kong Proceedings viz., Action No. 473 of 2026 before
the High Court of Hong Kong(SAR). 
Aggrieved  by  the  order  dated  24.08.2026,  the  Bankruptcy
Trustee filed the Special Leave Petition(C)No.33989 of 2026 before
this Court, contending that an order in the nature of an anti-suit
injunction ought not to have been passed at the behest of HDFC Bank
in the circumstances of the case.
When that Special Leave Petition came up for hearing on
01.10.2026, the only issue under consideration was whether the
order dated 24.08.2026 passed by the learned Single Judge of the
High Court in I.A.No.4412 of 2026 in Notice of Motion No. 763 of
2019 in Commercial Suit No. 157 of 2016, was justified or not.
The parties, who were at daggers drawn before us, were the
Bankruptcy Trustee on the one hand and the HDFC bank on the other.
After hearing the parties for some time, we passed the
following order and disposed of the Special Leave Petition on
01.10.2026:-

## Page 123

4
“1. Heard Mr. Santosh Paul, learned Senior Counsel for
the petitioners and Mr. Shyam Divan, learned Senior
Counsel appearing on caveat for contesting respondent-
HDFC Bank Limited. 
2. Having heard the submissions made by the learned
Senior Counsel for the parties, we are of the opinion,
that the contesting parties, namely, the petitioner(s)
and  HDFC  Bank  Limited,  should  sit  together  and
mediate.
3. Parties have favourably responded to the suggestion
of  the  Court  that  an  attempt  for  an  amicable
resolution to the dispute be explored through the
process of mediation.
4. We request to Hon’ble Justice Abhay S. Oka, Former
Judge of this Court to act as a Mediator in this
matter with the consent of both the parties. The
learned Mediator make an attempt to amicably resolved
the matter.
5. Parties to get in touch with the learned Mediator
and  appear  on  a  date  convenient  to  the  learned
Mediator.
6. The fees and other terms payable to the learned
Mediator shall be fixed in consultation with the
parties.
7. We are conscious that the proceedings are pending
before the High Court of Judicature at Bombay and we
notice that some applications are slated for hearing
on 05.10.2026 before the High Court.
8. The learned Mediator may, as and when the report is
ready, forwarded the same to the High Court in the
pending proceedings. The interim arrangement made by
the High Court shall continue till the mediation
proceedings conclude.
9. Learned counsel for the petitioner(s) submits that
the High Court proceeding may be stayed.
10. The pendency of mediation may be brought to the
notice of the High Court.
11. The Special Leave Petition is disposed of in the
above terms.
12. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand
disposed of.”
5. As is clear from the order passed by this Court on 01.10.2026,
we referred the matter to mediation before Hon’ble Mr. Justice

## Page 124

5
Abhay S.Oka, Former Judge of this Court, to mediate the dispute
between the Bankruptcy Trustee and the HDFC Bank.
6. The present application has been filed by the plaintiff
contending that he was not only the plaintiff in the suit but was
also arrayed as respondent no.2 in the Special Leave Petition filed
by the Bankruptcy Trustee and that he ought to have been heard
before passing the order.
7. Mr. Yatin Oza, learned Senior Counsel, submits that notice was
not issued to the respondent no.2 in the Special Leave Petition and
the matter was disposed of by referring the Bankruptcy Trustee and
the HDFC Bank to mediation.
8. On the other hand, Mr. Shyam Divan, learned Senior Counsel,
contends  that  the  applicant  has  no  locus  to  maintain  the
Miscellaneous Application or to participate in the mediation.
9. The dispute between the Bankruptcy Trustee and the HDFC Bank
was about the claim of HDFC Bank against the applicant herein, who
stood as a guarantor for a loan, to secure which the shares had
been pledged.
10. Mr. Divan, learned Senior Counsel, vehemently opposed the
participation of the applicant in the mediation.
11. Mr. Nachiketa Joshi, learned Senior Counsel appearing for the
Bankruptcy Trustee, submitted that once the Trustee had been
appointed, the applicant had no locus standi in the suit.
12. We are not concerned with any of the above disputes inter se
between the parties.
13. The narrow issue before us in the Special Leave Petition was
about the correctness of the order dated 24.08.2026 passed by the

## Page 125

6
High Court of Judicature at Bombay. It was in those circumstances
that  HDFC  Bank  and  the  Bankruptcy  Trustee  were  referred  to
mediation.
14. However, considering that the applicant, who is the plaintiff
in the suit and was respondent no.2 in the Special Leave Petition,
is desirous of participating in the mediation, we direct that the
applicant shall have the liberty to participate in the mediation
and place his case before the learned mediator.
15. Needless to say, this will not preclude the Bankruptcy Trustee
and the HDFC Bank from entering into any agreement, if so advised.
16. Needless to further observe, the applicant is always at
liberty to initiate such action or continue such proceedings, if
maintainable in law, to secure his rights, if any. 
17. We also notice that that the mediation has made significant
progress. The learned mediator has already concluded two sittings.
18. Our order dated 01.10.2026 does not, in any manner, adjudicate
on the existence or otherwise of any rights of the applicant
herein.
19. Our  order  also  does  not  discontinue  the  suit  bearing
Commercial  Suit  No.  157  of  2026.   Hence,  prayer  B  in  the
application is not tenable.
20. With  the  above  observations,  the  present  Miscellaneous
Application stands disposed of.
21. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
(VARSHA MENDIRATTA)                         (AKSHAY KUMAR BHORIA)

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL  NO(S). 3772/2017
ARYA SAMAJ (R) DAL BAZAARR                         APPELLANT(S)
                                VERSUS
JAGIR SINGH (D) THR LR                             RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. The present appeal has been filed assailing the impugned
judgement dated 17.01.2014 passed by the High Court of Punjab
and Haryana at Chandigarh in RSA No. 842/1987, whereby the
second appeal preferred by the respondent(s) was allowed, and
reversed the concurrent findings of the Trial Court and the
First Appellate Court.
2. Brief facts necessary for adjudicating the present appeal is
that the appellant before us is the plaintiff in the suit
bearing C.S. No. 214/1982. The suit was filed seeking the
relief of declaration and for possession of the suit premises
on the basis of a gift deed executed by one Late Shri Ganga
Ram dated 15.07.1969. 
3. Both the Trial Court and the First Appellate Court having

## Page 133

2
found that the Gift Deed, i.e., Exhibit P-5 was a registered
document, duly proved by the attesting witnesses and the
scribe, held that the plaintiff/appellant is entitled to the
reliefs prayed for and decreed the suit. 
4. On a second appeal filed by the defendant/respondent, the High
Court re-appreciated the evidence and without giving any
particular findings on perversity with respect to orders
passed by the subordinate Courts, arrived at a different
conclusion by fixing the onus upon the appellant who was
seeking the benefit of the Gift Deed (Exhibit-P-5). Aggrieved,
the present appeal has been filed. 
5. We have heard the learned counsel for the appellant and the
learned counsel appearing for the respondent and also perused
the impugned judgment dated 17.01.2014 passed by the High
Court. 
6. As stated in the narration of facts, the Trial Court and the
First  Appellate  Court  considered  the  issues  framed  and
accordingly answered in favour of the appellant. While the
Trial Court had the benefit of taking note of the demeanor of
the witnesses, the First Appellate Court being the final Court
of fact and law considered the relevant issues framed and
answered them accordingly.
7. We are conscious of the amendment made with respect to the
need of framing of a substantial question of law. In fact, the
High Court held that substantial question of law had been

## Page 134

3
answered. However, on a perusal of the impugned judgement, we
do not find any substantial question of law being dealt with
actually by the High Court, as the decision was passed upon
examination of facts. Furthermore, the High Court did not even
render its views on any perversity with the reasoning adopted
by the Trial Court and the First Appellate Court. 
8. In our considered view, the other reason given by the High
Court that the onus is on the appellant/plaintiff to prove the
gift deed, of which he seeks benefit, also cannot be taken
note of, especially, when the findings on facts have already
been given.
9. Taking note of the aforesaid, we are inclined to set aside the
impugned judgment passed by the High Court by remitting the
matter back to it for fresh consideration. 
10. All the issues are left open and, therefore, we request the
High Court to decide the second appeal on its own merits and
in accordance with law, without being influenced with any of
the previous findings. 
11. Taking into the facts of the case, since the suit was filed
way back in the year 1982, we request the High Court to decide
the second appeal within a period of six months from the date
of receipt of a copy of this order.  
12. The appeal stands allowed, accordingly.

1. Leave granted.
2. The  present  appeal  is  arising  out  of  the  order  dated
04.10.2019 passed by the High Court of Chhattisgarh in FA No.
13/2005 by which the appeal preferred by the Appellant-husband
dismissing a petition for grant of divorce has been dismissed.
3. The facts of the case reveal that the marriage took place
between the appellant and the respondent on 20.02.1988 and their
first child was born from the wedlock on 18.08.1989 and the second
child was born on 14.07.1991. Unfortunately, from July, 1991
onwards, the husband and wife started living separately and finally
in the year 1999, the appellant preferred a Divorce Petition under
Section 13(1)(i), 13(1)(ia) and 13(1)(ib) of Hindu Marriage Act.
Various allegations were leveled against respondent-wife and after
trial, the Divorce Petition was dismissed against which an appeal
has been preferred and the appeal has also been dismissed.
4. This  Court  has  made  a  number  of  attempts  for  amicable
settlement of the dispute between the parties however, all attempts
have resulted in failure.
5. This Court in the earlier round of litigation in Special Leave

## Page 143

2
Petition (C) No. 2504/2020 has directed the appellant-husband to
look after both the daughters till their marriage and today it has
been brought to the notice of this Court that one daughter has
already been married and the other daughter is employed, however,
no marriage has taken place in respect of second daughter.
6. Unfortunately, in spite of all attempts made by this Court,
there is no amicable settlement. Learned counsel for the appellant
has  stated  before  this  Court  that  the  parties  are  residing
separately for the last 35 years and it is irretrievable break down
of marriage. His contention is long separation of 35 years itself
is a good ground for grant of divorce keeping in view the judgment
of this Court in “Vikas Kanaujia vs. Sarita” reported in [(2025) 3
SCC 748].
7. Learned counsel for the appellant has also relied upon the
judgments in “Jatinder Kumar Sapra vs. Anupama Sapra” [(2024) 19
SCC 516], “P.P. Balakrishnan vs. Usha P.K.” [(2024) SCC Online SC
4036],  “Sonal Talpada vs. Veerbhan Singh” [(2026) 8 SCC 401)],
“Rajib Baheti vs. Sandesh Sharda” [(2025) 3 SCC 686)],  “Shilpa
Sailesh vs. Varun Sreenivasan” [(2023) 14 SCC 231] and “Samar Ghosh
vs. Jaya Ghosh” [(2007) 4 SCC 511)].
8. Learned counsel for the appellant further stated before this
Court that the appellant is a pensioner. He was working as
electrician and now he is surviving on a meager amount of pension.
Learned counsel for the appellant offered a sum of Rs. 20,00,000/-
(Rs. Twenty Lakh only) to be paid to the respondent-wife by way of
lump sum payment towards maintenance and all other claims made by
the wife.

## Page 144

3
9. On the other hand, learned counsel for the respondent-wife has
argued  before  this  Court  that  the  husband  has  made  serious
allegations against the wife in the Divorce Petition, therefore,
the appeal be dismissed. He has also admitted the fact that one of
the daughters is married now and the other daughter is gainfully
employed. He has vehemently opposed the prayer for grant of
divorce.
10. This Court after hearing learned counsel for the parties is of
the opinion that instead of Rs. 20,00,000/- (Rs. Twenty Lakh only)
an amount of Rs. 25,00,000/- (Rs. Twenty Five Lakh only) be paid to
the respondent-wife within a period of four months from today and
the daughter who is unemployed be paid a sum of Rs. 5,00,000/- (Rs.
Five Lakh only) within a period of four weeks.
11. At this stage, learned counsel for the appellant has also
informed this court that the agricultural land owned by the
appellant is in the possession of the respondent-wife and wife is
approximately earning Rs. 4 to 5 lakhs per year from the land in
question.
12. In light of the aforesaid, it is directed that till the wife
is alive, the wife will not be dispossessed from the land and
income arising out of the agricultural land will also go to the
wife as she is looking after the agricultural land.
13. All disputes between the parties will come to an end.
14. This Court in light of the aforesaid facts and circumstances
and the directions issued in the present case in exercise of powers
conferred under Article 142 of the Constitution of India and the
judicial precedents referred herein, grant the decree of divorce on

106-A/2004 and the judgment dated 04.10.2019 passed by the High
Court of Chhattisgarh in FA No. 13 of 2005 are hereby set aside.

under Article 142 of the Constitution of India. Learned counsel for
the appellant in open court has also withdrawn all allegations made
in the Divorce Petition against the wife.
15. The present Civil Appeal is allowed accordingly.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
EXTRAORDINARY APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Special Leave Petition (Crl.) No.531 of 2026
POOJA RANI                                       
Petitioner(s)
VERSUS
STATE OF HARYANA & ANR.    Respondent(s)
O R D E R
The petitioner is aggrieved with the impugned
order of the High Court of Punjab & Haryana at
Chandigarh;  which  we  are  of  the  opinion  is
perfectly in order, especially considering the
manner  in  which  allegations  are  made  of
molestation and sexual intercourse on the promise
of marriage, which are then later settled, by the
sheer  coercion  exerted  on  such  criminal
proceedings  being  initiated  and  continued.
However,  we  intend  to  slightly  modify  the
directions issued.
2. The  petitioner,  a  31-year-old  woman,
registered an FIR on 12.01.2024, alleging that
while she was tending to her brother admitted in
a  hospital,  the  respondent  offered  his
assistance, and on that pretext, became intimate
with her and coerced her into sexual intercourse;
which  even  according  to  her,  she  willingly
complied believing that he would marry her, which
he promised. She also alleged that the parents of
the respondent also met her and there was a sort
of ceremony conducted and then later she was
abandoned. 

## Page 148

2
3. A settlement was arrived at, in which the
respondent  promised  to  pay  an  amount  of
Rs.9,25,000/-, of which, Rs.4,50,000/- was paid.
The High Court found that the very perusal of the
record  prima facie  reveals a  mala fide  case,
especially when the petitioner is a mature woman
who was fully conscious of her act and conduct.
By making allegations of sexual harassment on the
pretext of marriage, she had put into motion the
criminal justice machinery, which according to
the High Court; undermines the sanctity of the
legal process.
4. The  High  Court  observed  that  the  Courts
should not become instruments of undue pressure,
leading to extortion from one party and illegal
enrichment of another. To preserve the integrity
of the criminal justice system, the High Court
set  aside  the  settlement  and  made  it
unenforceable with respect to the balance amounts
payable to the petitioner. The High Court also
directed  that  the  proceedings  initiated  under
Section 13B of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955,
shall be proceeded with and if the petitioner
resiles from her consent before the Family Court,
appropriate proceedings shall be taken against
her;  meaning  perjury.  The  High  Court  also
directed an exemplary cost of Rs.5,00,000/- to be
imposed on the petitioner and directed it to be
paid to two entities, one established in the care
of women and the other, a fund established for

## Page 149

3
poor patients. 
5. We are perfectly in agreement with the High
Court that such nefarious practices undermining
the judicial system has to be deprecated in the
strongest  of  terms.  Only  in  the  facts  and
circumstances of the case, we modify the order to
the extent of deleting the penalty imposed on the
petitioner; but cautioning her in the strongest
of  terms  from  indulging  in  such  activities
hereinafter. 
6. Insofar as the settlement is concerned, we
confirm the order of the High Court which made it
unenforceable against the party respondent. 
7. As far as the proceedings before the Family
Court,  we  deem  it  fit,  in  the  facts  and
circumstances of the case, to grant divorce to
the parties invoking our powers under Article 142
of the Constitution of India, finding from the
facts  and  circumstances,  an  irretrievable
breakdown of marriage.
8. The Special Leave Petition is disposed of
with the above directions.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
rejected.

measuring about 5.0 m x 3.5 m, between Gandhi Nagar, Sector-13 and
Heeradas  Kunda  drains,  passing  through  the  Central  Nursery,
involving diversion of 0.1272 hectares of protected forest land.
3. A joint inspection was conducted on 03.02.2025 pursuant to
which, the Deputy Conservator of Forests, Bharatpur, recorded that
no work had commenced without sanction and recommended the project,
subject to grant of permission from this Court for felling of
trees. The proposal for prior approval of the Central Government
for diversion of the forest land is also stated to have been
submitted on the PARIVESH Portal. The Applicant has undertaken to
plant 510 saplings, i.e. ten times the number of trees proposed to
be felled towards compensatory afforestation.
4. While issuing notice on 23.02.2026, this Court directed that a
copy  of  this  application  be  supplied  to  CEC  for  its
recommendations.
5. Pursuant thereto, CEC has filed Report No. 14 of 2026 dated
17.07.2026,  thereby recommending that 49 trees can be felled
instead of 51, i.e. Serial Nos. 19 and 41, can be saved. Further,
as the identified land can accommodate 510 saplings, CEC has
retained the proposal made by the Applicant to plant 510 saplings

for compensatory plantation as against the requirement of 490

6. Ms. Liz Mathew, learned Senior Counsel and Amicus Curiae, in

that the diversion of 0.1272 hectares of protected forest land
would require prior approval of the Central Government in view of
Section 2(1)(ii) of the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam,
1980.
7. We agree with the conditions recommended by the learned Amicus
in paragraphs 6 and 7 of her note.
8. Consequently, we allow these applications with the direction

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The instant Writ Petition under Article 32 of the Constitution 
was entertained purely on humanitarian considerations, in view of 
the extraordinary circumstances of the case. The petitioner’s 
husband, Captain Ashish Kumar, a Master in the Merchant Navy, had 
joined the merchant vessel M.T. Skylight at Dubai on 22.01.2026. On 
01.03.2026, the vessel is stated to have come under a missile/drone 
attack in the Strait of Hormuz and caught fire.
2. On 02.03.2026, the petitioner was informed by the Embassy of 
India in Muscat, Oman, that eight Indian crew members had been 
rescued by the Omani authorities. Two others, namely, her husband 
and one Dilip Singh, were reported missing, as they were stated to 
be in the engine room at the time of the incident.
3. Subsequently, on 03.03.2026, the Embassy communicated that the 
two missing persons were likely deceased. The next day, the 
petitioner was informed that burnt skeletal remains had been 
recovered from the Captain’s cabin, one of which was presumed to be 
that of her husband.
4. The petitioner states that, on the same day, she received 
calls on her WhatsApp number from unknown persons using foreign and 
Indian phone numbers. The callers apparently claimed that her 
husband was alive and demanded a ransom of Rs. 20 lakhs.

## Page 159

3
5. According to the petitioner, the Biological Technological 
Report received on 12.03.2026 from the Directorate General of 
Search  and  Criminal  Investigation,  Royal  Oman  Police,  was 
inconclusive.  Her  husband’s  brother,  Akash  Kumar,  thereafter 
travelled  to  Oman  and  provided  a  DNA  sample  on  21.04.2026, 
whereupon it was confirmed that the skeletal remains were not those 
of her husband. Representations were also made by the petitioner’s 
father-in-law to the police authorities on 06.04.2026 and to the 
Prime  Minister’s  Office  on  22.05.2026,  seeking  a  detailed 
investigation into the whereabouts of her husband. The petitioner 
avers that her husband is in illegal captivity.
6. It is in these circumstances that we had initially intervened 
and deemed it appropriate to issue notice to the Union of India.
7. The Union of India has since informed us that, despite its 
best efforts through diplomatic channels, it has not been able to 
ascertain the whereabouts of the petitioner’s husband, and that the 
information available indicates that he may no longer be alive.
8. The petitioner has, however, placed before us today a video 
clip which, according to her, shows her husband in an injured 
condition. She asserts that her husband is alive, and that if 
sincere efforts are made by the authorities, his whereabouts can be 
traced and he can be brought back safely.

## Page 160

4
9. There is no gainsaying that the material now relied upon by 
the petitioner would require due verification by the agencies 
concerned, in coordination with foreign authorities. We, therefore, 
dispose of this writ petition with the following directions:
(i) As undertaken, the petitioner shall hand over the video clip 
and any other new material to learned Counsel for the Union of 
India during the course of the day. 
(ii) Upon receipt, the authorities concerned shall verify the 
genuineness of the video clip. If there is reason to believe that 
the person in the video clip is the petitioner’s husband, the 
authorities shall take up the matter through the appropriate 
diplomatic channels to trace his whereabouts and to secure his safe 
return.
(iii) While in such like matters, which involve liaisoning with 
foreign authorities, we refrain from fixing a timeline. However, we 
expect the authorities to make sincere efforts to comply with the 
letter and spirit of these directions.
10. I.A.  No.  308374/2026  is  dismissed,  with  liberty  to  the 
petitioner to approach the appropriate authorities or forum in 
respect of the reliefs sought therein.
11. The writ petition is, accordingly, disposed of in the above 
terms. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The  statement  reportedly  published  by  the  respondent  herein
through its official social media account reads thus:
“Dear Surya Kant, If law and order is not your domain,
resign now. We will find your replacement who can
handle it.”
1

## Page 162

2. The screenshot of the said publication has been enclosed with the
representation dated 13.10.2026 submitted by Mr. Vineet Jindal, Advocate.
3. The present matter concerns certain remarks directed against the
Hon’ble Chief Justice of India attributed in the social media account of a
political organization namely the respondent herein.
4. The  Constitution  is  supreme.  No  individual,  no  institution  or
political organization stands above. The independence of judiciary is not a
matter  of  political  convenience.  It  is  a  constitutional  guarantee  to  the
people of this Republic.
5. Judgments are always open to criticism, however severe. Freedom
of expression cannot become a shield for intimidation or interference with
the  administration  of  justice.  Howsoever  high  position  a  person  may
occupy, such person cannot be allowed to pollute the stream of justice.
Judicial restraint must never be mistaken for institutional weakness. Any
attempt to undermine the authority of the Court requires to be dealt with
iron hand.
6. The authority of this Court requires neither political endorsement or
approval from any party. It rests upon the Constitution and the Rule of
Law. Where interference with the administration of justice is established,
the law must take its course, irrespective of identity or influence of the
persons of those who are responsible.
7. Having  regard  to  the  nature  of  allegations,  we  consider  it
appropriate  to  examine  whether  the  material  warrants  exercise  of  this
Court’s jurisdiction under Article 129 of the Constitution of India.
2

## Page 163

8. Hence, we hereby appoint Shri Arvind P Datar and Mr. Gaurav
Agrawal, learned Senior Counsels as Amicus Curiae to assist the Court for
the  questions  arising  for  consideration  and  to  examine  as  to  whether
criminal contempt or civil contempt requires to be initiated in the facts
obtained and who should be brought under the umbrella of Contempt of
Courts Act, 1971.
9. We also request the learned Attorney General to assist the Court.
The Registry shall furnish a complete set of papers to the learned Amicus
Curiae and learned Attorney General forthwith. We clarify that we have not
expressed any opinion on the merits of the allegations, at this stage.
10. Hence, we issue notice to all the office bearers of Kerala Pradesh
Congress Committee and show cause as to why the proceedings under the
Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 should not be initiated? Mr. Ramesh Babu,
learned Senior Counsel along with Shri Subash Chandran, learned counsel
representing Subash Chandran & Kavitha Law Associates (AOR) accepts
notice and waives notice for all the respondents. He would also hasten to
add that at this juncture notice to all the office bearers may not be issued,
but it may be confined only to the President of the Kerala Pradesh Congress
Committee and he would further add that contemnor would be tendering an
unconditional and unqualified apology for the material uploaded on the
official social media handle (‘X’) of the contemnor.
11. At this juncture, we do not propose to confine our order of issuing
notice only to the President of the Kerala Pradesh Congress Committee but
all the office bearers of the contemnor. As such, we issue notice to all the
3

## Page 164

office bearers of Kerala Pradesh Congress Committee to show cause as to
why  proceedings  under  Contempt  of  Courts  Act,  1971  should  not  be
initiated against them. Mr. Subash Chandran & Kavitha Law Associates
(AOR) accepts and waives service of notice on the office bearers of Kerala
Pradesh Congress Committee. 
12. Notwithstanding  the  acceptance  of  notice,  since  this  Court  is
exercising jurisdiction under Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 notice is being
issued to all the office bearers of Kerala Pradesh Congress Committee and
we direct the Registry to issue the notice to all the office bearers of Kerala
Pradesh  Congress  Committee.  For  the  present  we  exempt  from  their
personal appearance.
13. List on 15.12.2026.

O R D E R
1. In course of hearing of this transfer petition, the petitioner-wife
(Neha  Rajendra  Chandak)  and  the  respondent-husband  (Mohit
Sharma) were referred to the Supreme Court Mediation Centre.
2. The process of mediation has produced positive results. The
Mediator has sent a report that the parties have agreed to resolve the
inter se disputes and differences amicably. It has also been decided
by  them  to  apply  before  this  Court  seeking  dissolution  of  their
marriage by mutual consent under Article 142 of the Constitution of
India.
3. The parties have jointly filed an application under Article 142
of the Constitution of India in Court, which is taken on record. The
prayers in the application under Article 142 read as follows:
“a) Take on record the Settlement Agreement dated 21.09.2026
executed at the Supreme Court Mediation Centre (Annexure A-
2),  direct  the  parties  to  abide  by  the  terms  and  conditions
thereof, and accept the undertakings of the parties contained
therein as undertakings given to this Hon’ble Court ;
b) Allow the present joint application filed under Article 142 of the
Constitution of India and grant a decree of divorce by mutual
consent under Section 13-B of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955,
1

## Page 170

dissolving  the  marriage  solemnized  between  the  Petitioner-
wife,  Dr.  Neha  Rajendra  Chandak,  and  the  Respondent-
husband,  Dr.  Mohit  Sharma,  on  03.12.2017  at  Nagpur,
Maharashtra, dispensing with the procedure and waiving off the
statutory cooling of period prescribed under in the said Act;
c)   Direct that HMA Petition No.2315 of 2025 titled “Mohit Sharma
V. Neha Chandak” pending before the Ld. Family Court, Tis
Hazari Courts, Delhi shall stand disposed of in terms of the
Settlement Agreement, and that all other proceedings, civil or
criminal,  if  any,  between  the  parties  arising  out  of  their
matrimonial relationship shall stand quashed;
d) Dispose of Transfer Petition (Civil) No.135 of 2026 in terms of
the Settlement Agreement dated 21.09.2026; and 
e) pass such other or further order(s)/direction(s) as this Hon'ble
Court may deem fit and proper in the facts and circumstances
of the case.”
 
4. During the course of the dispute, the parties filed the below
mentioned cases against each other:
i) Transfer Petition (Civil) No.135 of 2026 titled “Neha Rajendra
Chandak Vs. Mohit Sharma”, i.e., the present proceedings, pending
before this Hon’ble Court; and
ii) HMA Petition No.2315 of 2025 titled “Mohit Sharma Vs. Neha
Chandak”, pending before the Ld. Family Court, Tis Hazari Courts,
Delhi.
5. We have interacted with the petitioner  and the respondent
today,  who  have  joined  the  proceedings  virtually.  They  have
separately submitted, while responding to our query, that they have
agreed to part ways without any threat, force, coercion or undue
influence.  We  record  their  further  statement  that  the  mutual
obligations as per the settlement dated 27th October, 2026 have been
worked out.
6. The parties having amicably resolved the inter se disputes and
differences, the terms of settlement contained in the joint application
shall form part of this order.

CIVIL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION
TRANSFER PETITION   (C) No.308/2026  
ZEENAT JABI PETITIONER
VERSUS
SUHAIL AHMAD RESPONDENT
O R D E R
1. Read the office report dated 03rd November, 2026.
2. This  transfer petition,  under Section  25 of the  Code  of Civil
Procedure, 1908, has been presented by the petitioner-wife, Zeenat
Jabi.
3. The  marriage  between  the  petitioner  and  the  respondent-
husband, Suhail Ahmad, was solemnized on 25th May, 2025. No child
was born to the petitioner and the respondent from the wedlock.
However, the parties have since drifted apart owing to differences
arising by and between them.
4. The respondent has instituted proceedings under Section 34 of
the Specific Relief Act, 1963 r/w Section 7(1)(a) Explanation (b) & (d)
of the Family Court Act, 1984 for Declaration of the Dissolution of
Marriage under Muslim Personal Law (Talaq-UL-Sunnat) bearing Suit
No.125 of 2025 titled “Suhail Ahmad vs. Zeenat Jabi” in the court of
1

## Page 174

the Principal Judge, Family Courts, District South-East, Saket Courts,
Delhi.
5. On the multiple grounds urged in the petition, the petitioner has
sought for transfer of the aforesaid proceedings to the court of the
Principal Judge, Family Court, District Bijnor, Uttar Pradesh.
6. We have heard learned counsel for the parties.
7. We  are  satisfied,  having  regard  to  the  inconvenience  the
petitioner is likely to face if the proceedings were continued before
the Principal Judge, Family Courts, District South-East, Saket Courts,
Delhi, that  interest  of  justice  demands  grant  of  the  prayer  for
transfer.
8. Hence, the  transfer  petition  is  allowed.  Suit  No.125  of 2025
titled  “Suhail Ahmad vs. Zeenat Jabi” pending before  the Principal
Judge,  Family  Courts,  District  South-East,  Saket  Courts,  Delhi is
transferred to the court of the Principal Judge, Family Court, District
Bijnor, Uttar Pradesh. Records of Suit No.125 of 2025 be transferred
to the transferee court immediately.
9. To avoid delay, the parties are directed to appear before the
transferee court on 08th December, 2026. If any or both the parties
fail to appear on that day, the presiding officer of the transferee
court will fix another date for appearance. Thereafter, he shall be
free to proceed in accordance with law.
10. Notwithstanding that mediation has failed, the presiding officer
of the transferee court shall endeavour to bring about a settlement
between the parties through the process of mediation. If the process
2

## Page 175

is  unsuccessful  once  again,  nothing  shall  preclude  the  presiding
officer to take the proceedings to its logical conclusion on its merits
and in accordance with law.
11. As  per  the  last  order  dated  13th August,  2026,  it  has  been
reported that video conferencing facility is available at the Family
Court, District Bijnor, Uttar Pradesh.
12. Hence, if the respondent is unable to attend the proceedings in
person on any occasion, he will be at liberty to seek permission to
attend through the virtual mode and if such a permission is sought,
the  presiding  officer  of  the  court  may  proceed  to  consider  it
reasonably.
